introduction.title: WPN — From Wastewater Concentrations to Chemical Priorities
paragraphs: WPN combines wastewater monitoring, exposure modelling and biological effect potency to prioritize neurotoxic chemicals. Explore the study below, then enter concentrations for your own selection of the 52 target chemicals.

sections.title: A wastewater-based model platform
paragraphs: The study maps neurotoxic chemical mixture burdens across 117 urban areas in 18 European countries. It asks whether the chemicals most abundant in wastewater are also those contributing most strongly after exposure translation, toxicokinetics and potency are considered.

The framework links wastewater concentration (WW), estimated daily exposure (DE), internal-equivalent concentration (Cb) and narciclasine-equivalent bioanalytical equivalent concentration (BEQ). The platform applies this model to user-provided WW concentrations and presents chemical priorities as BEQ rankings and contributions.

sections.title: Selecting the 52 target chemicals
paragraphs: The literature inventory contains 1,554 candidates: 1,199 from the reference study and 355 additional literature-derived chemicals. Ninety-seven have positive numerical relative effect potencies (REPs) for neurite-outgrowth inhibition. The NORMAN inventory contains 1,035 chemical records. Applying urban-coverage and correlation-support criteria yields a 663-chemical reconstruction background; its overlap with the 97 positive-REP candidates contains 53 chemicals. Excluding endogenous creatinine gives the 52 exogenous targets.

The panel comprises 23 aromatic polar organics, 2 bisphenols, 2 halogenated persistent organics, 8 organophosphorus compounds, 1 PFAS, 1 phthalate, 9 non-halogenated small polar organics and 6 surfactants or quaternary ammonium compounds. All 52 have positive REP values and the toxicokinetic parameters used for BEQ calculation.

sections.title: Biological context
paragraphs: ExposomeX E-BIO describes recorded chemical–disease associations through exposure–protein–protein–disease (EPPD) and exposure–Gene Ontology–disease (EGoD) networks. The 52 targets connect to 246 of 261 diseases in EPPD and 198 of 278 in EGoD, corresponding to 94.25% and 71.22% coverage.

A separate mechanism-overlap analysis draws random sets of 52 chemicals from each disease's associated pool. Across eligible diseases, these sets cover an average 71.44% of proteins and 72.04% of Gene Ontology terms.

sections.title: Wastewater monitoring and concentration reconstruction
paragraphs: Georeferenced NORMAN monitoring records were matched to Global Urban Boundary (GUB) morphological urban areas using point-in-polygon matching and documented station-to-city assignments. Records within an urban area were summarized as chemical-specific medians.

The 117 × 663 concentration matrix contains 12,746 observations and 64,825 missing combinations (83.57%). TabPFN-assisted sequential reconstruction uses other chemical concentrations, missingness indicators and co-occurrence features to estimate missing values, while retaining the observations. Bounded residual sampling supplies variability to reconstructed values. Extracting the 52 targets yields 6,084 city–chemical values: 1,408 observed and 4,676 reconstructed.

sections.title: Reconstruction validation
paragraphs: Ten repeated masking tests, each withholding approximately 10% of observations, produce 12,750 predictions from 8,339 distinct observed cells. On the log10(nM) scale, pooled R² is 0.783, RMSE is 0.455 and MAE is 0.321.

Predictions from the earlier A1 dataset compared with 1,062 newly available A2 observations give R² = 0.635. The completed A1 and A2 matrices have R² = 0.905 across 35,340 shared combinations. In observation-thinning tests, mean R² remains 0.590 after removing 75% of observations under the study's support criteria.

sections.title: The wastewater-to-exposure model
paragraphs: The WW–DE model draws on an external regional resource containing 11,217 records for 1,116 substances across 90 countries or regions. Chemical-level aggregation and exclusion of single-region chemicals yield 472 modelling units. Predictors are log10 wastewater concentration in μM and three IFSQSAR descriptors: reference-fish biotransformation half-life (fhlb), logSoliquid and logSwliquid. The response is log10 daily exposure in μmol/day, derived from SEEM3 estimates at a standardized body mass of 70 kg.

The fitted TabPFN regressor uses training-derived median filling and standardization. Chemical-level tenfold cross-validation gives pooled R² = 0.508, RMSE = 1.039 and MAE = 0.753 on the log10 scale. Permutation importance, wastewater perturbations from 0.1× to 10× and a comparison of 12 candidate models examine feature influence and model performance.

sections.title: From exposure to BEQ
paragraphs: The model translates predicted daily exposure using a standardized single-compartment, steady-input calculation and chemical-specific ADMETlab elimination half-life and volume of distribution. Multiplying the internal-equivalent concentration by molar REP gives narciclasine-equivalent BEQ. Values are expressed in μg/L narciclasine-EQ using narciclasine's molecular mass of 307.25 g/mol.

Exposure translation and effect potency change the chemical priorities. Across-city median ranks shift priority stratum for 21 of 52 chemicals from WW to DE and for 26 from DE to BEQ. Mean WW and BEQ top-ten lists share only two chemicals. BIT ranks 23rd by mean WW and first by mean BEQ, contributing 92.03% of the across-city mean total.

sections.title: Mixture burdens across European cities
paragraphs: Total model-derived BEQ ranges from 7.281 × 10⁻⁶ to 8.515 × 10⁻⁶ μg/L narciclasine-EQ across the 117 urban areas, a 1.170-fold range. BIT contributes 90.33–93.33% within individual cities.

Summarizing the remaining chemicals after excluding BIT reveals secondary contributors including gabapentin, 1,3-diphenylguanidine and quaternary ammonium compounds. Their combined BEQ ranges from 5.254 × 10⁻⁷ to 8.123 × 10⁻⁷ μg/L. The study also examines chemical-class totals and average BEQ per class member.

sections.title: National food-supply context
paragraphs: An exploratory analysis compares national wastewater medians with 2015–2019 median FAOSTAT food-supply quantities for 71 food items across 18 countries. The analysis covers 3,692 chemical–food pairs, food-module patterns, country-label permutations and global false-discovery-rate correction.

The main text and supplementary analysis report 201 positive correlations with ρ ≥ 0.5, 3.06-fold above the permutation mean, and four globally significant pairs. These national associations provide context for subsequent source investigations.

sections.title: Supporting evidence for priority chemicals
paragraphs: The BIT evidence synthesis brings together environmental bioassays, human biomonitoring, household-product use and animal toxicokinetics. The combined evidence supports targeted measurement and paired chemical–bioassay validation of priority chemicals.
Extended Data Fig. 6 provides an additional historical comparison of 42 matched chemicals using DeepToxLab-weighted scores and HExpPredict estimates.

sections.title: Using the platform
paragraphs: Chemical provides names, identifiers, categories and details for the 52 target chemicals. In WPN, add chemicals individually, paste two columns from Excel or upload a spreadsheet. Enter WW concentrations in nM and preview the recognized records. Use Example data to try the workflow with concentrations derived from the study's 117-city medians.

Run the valid records to calculate your results. Only chemicals with a supplied valid concentration participate. Rank opens the BEQ chart with cumulative contributions; Data contains the values and a CSV download. My results shows your most recent calculation, while Study results displays the paper's mean BEQ ranking for all 52 chemicals.

chemical.title: Chemical — The 52 Target Chemicals
paragraphs: Explore the identities and categories of the 52 chemicals available for WPN calculations.

sections.title: Why these chemicals?
paragraphs: The target panel combines wastewater monitoring coverage with numerical evidence of neurite-outgrowth inhibition. The literature-derived inventory comprised 1,554 candidate chemicals, including 97 with positive numerical relative effect potency (REP) values for this endpoint. The NORMAN wastewater archive contained 1,035 chemicals, of which 663 were measured in at least three study urban areas. Intersecting these 663 chemicals with the 97 positive-REP candidates yielded 53 compounds. Excluding endogenous creatinine gave the final panel of 52 exogenous target chemicals.
The panel spans eight chemical categories. Each target has the potency and toxicokinetic parameters needed to translate a wastewater concentration into BEQ.

sections.title: Find a chemical
paragraphs: Use a chemical name, CAS number or InChIKey in Data; the three selectors stay synchronized. The table lists chemical identities and categories, and Details provides synonyms, molecular formula, molecular weight and REP. Download CSV exports the chemicals shown by the current filter.

wpn.title: WPN — Enter Concentrations and Run the Model
paragraphs: Calculate BEQ priorities for any selection of the 52 target chemicals using your wastewater concentrations.

sections.title: 1. Enter your concentrations
paragraphs: Add chemicals individually using a name, CAS number or InChIKey, or bring in two columns from Excel: chemical identifier and WW concentration. Concentrations use nM and must be positive numbers. You can enter one chemical or any combination up to the full 52.
Example data loads the study-derived concentrations so you can try the workflow. Edited values are highlighted. Figure shows the concentrations currently entered.

sections.title: 2. Preview and run
paragraphs: The preview separates valid and invalid records and identifies any issues. Use Back to edit your data or upload again, or run the valid chemicals. Chemicals without a supplied valid concentration are left out.

sections.title: 3. Explore your results
paragraphs: When the calculation finishes, Rank opens your BEQ chart. Explore individual and cumulative contributions, view the full result table or download the values. After changing your inputs, run WPN again to update the results.

rank.title: Rank — BEQ Priorities and Contributions
paragraphs: Identify the chemicals contributing most strongly to the modelled mixture effect.

sections.title: Read your results
paragraphs: My results ranks the chemicals in your latest calculation from highest to lowest BEQ, expressed in μg/L narciclasine-EQ. Each chemical's contribution is its BEQ divided by the total BEQ of the chemicals evaluated in that calculation.

Figure shows BEQ bars and a cumulative contribution line. The left axis uses a logarithmic scale by default and can be switched to a linear scale; the right axis shows cumulative percentage. Drag the bottom slider handles to zoom and its middle area to move through the chemicals. Data provides Rank, Chemical, WW input, BEQ and Contribution (%).

sections.title: Study results
paragraphs: Study results displays the paper's 52-chemical ranking by mean BEQ across 117 cities. BIT ranks first and contributes 92.03% of the mean total. Switch between My results and Study results using the two buttons above the chart or table.

citation.text: Fu, N. et al. Mapping Neurotoxic Mixture Burdens Across European Cities.

paragraphs: Scientific sources include NORMAN wastewater monitoring, GUB and GeoNames urban data, SEEM3 exposure estimates, IFSQSAR descriptors, ADMETlab parameters, published neurite-outgrowth potencies, FAOSTAT and ExposomeX E-BIO.
